key_terms.meaning: An isolated system is described by a unit vector |ψ⟩ (a ray) in a complex Hilbert space
A closed system evolves by a unitary operator: |ψ(t)⟩ = U|ψ(0)⟩, with U†U = I
A measurement is a set of operators {Mₘ} with Σ Mₘ†Mₘ = I; outcome m has probability p(m) = ⟨ψ|Mₘ†Mₘ|ψ⟩
The state space of two systems is the tensor product V ⊗ W of their spaces
A two-level quantum system; its state is a unit vector α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with |α|² + |β|² = 1
The complex coefficient α or β in front of a basis state; its squared modulus is a probability
A state written as a linear combination Σ αᵢ|i⟩ of basis states, existing before measurement
The angle between two complex amplitudes; it changes interference, unlike a global phase
The unit sphere on which every pure qubit state sits at polar angle θ and azimuth φ
Probability of outcome m is p(m) = ⟨ψ|Pₘ|ψ⟩ = |⟨m|ψ⟩|² for a projective measurement
A measurement given by orthogonal projectors Pₘ with Σ Pₘ = I; after outcome m the state becomes Pₘ|ψ⟩/√p(m)
ρ = Σ pᵢ|ψᵢ⟩⟨ψᵢ|, Hermitian, positive, with trace 1; describes pure and mixed states alike
The operation ⊗ that builds a joint state |a⟩⊗|b⟩ in a space of dimension d₁d₂ from two subsystems
ρ_A = Tr_B(ρ_AB); it discards subsystem B and can turn a pure joint state into a mixed local state
A joint state that cannot be written as |a⟩⊗|b⟩ for any states of the parts
One of the four maximally entangled two-qubit states, e.g. |Φ⁺⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2
For local hidden variables, S = E(a,b) − E(a,b′) + E(a′,b) + E(a′,b′) satisfies |S| ≤ 2
The largest quantum value of the CHSH expression, |S| = 2√2 ≈ 2.828
Silver atoms through a non-uniform magnetic field split into exactly two beams, showing quantised spin
For observables A, B: ΔA·ΔB ≥ ½|⟨[A,B]⟩|, so non-commuting observables cannot both be sharp

takeaways: Four postulates — state vector, unitary evolution, measurement rule and tensor products — are the whole grammar of quantum computing.
A classical bit holds 0 or 1; a qubit holds two complex amplitudes and still hands back only one bit when measured.
Superposition is linear addition of amplitudes, and relative phase decides whether amplitudes add or cancel.
Every pure qubit state is a point on the Bloch sphere, so single-qubit gates are rotations of that sphere.
Measurement is probabilistic (Born rule) and disturbs the state; the outcome statistics come from the amplitudes, not from ignorance.
A pure state of a joint system can look mixed on one side once you trace out the other side.
Entanglement means the whole has definite properties that the parts separately do not have.
Bell's inequality and the CHSH game turn that statement into a number: local realism stops at 2, quantum mechanics reaches 2√2.
Stern–Gerlach showed that spin is quantised and that measuring one component destroys sharpness in another.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually built around stating a postulate and then using it: syllabi stress the postulates, the Bloch sphere, the Born rule, density matrices and the Bell/CHSH violation, with Stern–Gerlach used as the physical illustration.

bank.q: State the four postulates of quantum mechanics and explain what each one says about state, evolution, measurement and composite systems.
outline: Postulate 1: state is a unit vector |ψ⟩ in a complex Hilbert space; global phase is unobservable.
Postulate 2: closed-system evolution is unitary, |ψ(t)⟩ = U|ψ(0)⟩, U†U = I; it is reversible.
Postulate 3: measurement is a set {Mₘ} with Σ Mₘ†Mₘ = I; probability p(m) = ⟨ψ|Mₘ†Mₘ|ψ⟩, post-measurement state Mₘ|ψ⟩/√p(m).
Postulate 4: composite space is the tensor product of the component spaces.
One line on why the postulates matter: every circuit, gate and algorithm is written using only these four.

bank.q: Compare a classical bit with a quantum bit. What information does a qubit carry before and after measurement?
outline: Classical bit: one of two values, 0 or 1; can be copied freely; reading does not change it.
Qubit: unit vector α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with α, β complex and |α|² + |β|² = 1.
Measurement in the {|0⟩, |1⟩} basis returns 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with probability |β|².
Before measurement the amplitudes can carry more descriptive content; after measurement only one classical bit remains.
Contrast: n bits hold one of 2ⁿ strings; n qubits hold 2ⁿ amplitudes but yield n bits per measurement.

bank.q: Explain superposition and relative phase in quantum states, and show how phase controls interference.
outline: Define a basis, then a superposition Σ αᵢ|i⟩ with Σ|αᵢ|² = 1.
Example: |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 and |−⟩ = (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2 differ only in relative phase.
Global phase e^{iγ}|ψ⟩ gives identical statistics; relative phase between two amplitudes is observable.
Interference: amplitudes add before squaring, so a relative phase of π cancels a path.
Hadamard on |0⟩ and on |1⟩ as a concrete demonstration.

bank.q: Describe the Stern–Gerlach experiment and explain what it shows about quantised spin and about measurement.
outline: Silver atoms in a non-uniform magnetic field deflect by a force proportional to the spin component along the field.
Classically a continuous smear is expected; two spots are seen, so the component takes only two values ±ħ/2.
A second analyser along the same axis repeats the first result; a second analyser along a perpendicular axis splits the beam again.
Reversing the order destroys the earlier sharpness: the measurement disturbs the state.
Link to Pauli matrices, to incompatible observables and to the uncertainty principle.

bank.q: Starting from |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, derive the Bloch sphere coordinates and place |0⟩, |1⟩, |+⟩ and |+i⟩ on the sphere.
outline: Remove the global phase: write α = cos(θ/2)e^{−iφ/2}, β = sin(θ/2)e^{+iφ/2}.
State |ψ⟩ = cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + e^{iφ}sin(θ/2)|1⟩.
Map to the Bloch vector (sin θ cos φ, sin θ sin φ, cos θ), with 0 ≤ θ ≤ π and 0 ≤ φ < 2π.
Placement: |0⟩ at the north pole, |1⟩ at the south pole, |+⟩ on +x, |+i⟩ on +y.
Note that orthogonal states are antipodal and that global phase does not move the point.

bank.q: A qubit is in the state |ψ⟩ = (√3/2)|0⟩ + (1/2)|1⟩. Compute the probabilities of the outcomes of a measurement in the Z basis, then in the X basis.
outline: Z basis: p(0) = |√3/2|² = 3/4, p(1) = |1/2|² = 1/4; probabilities sum to one.
State the post-measurement state in each case and note the Bloch vector component along the measured axis.

bank.q: For the Bell state |Φ⁺⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, write the density matrix and take the partial trace over one qubit. Interpret the result.
outline: Trace out qubit B: ρ_A = Tr_B ρ, computed by summing the diagonal blocks over B's index.
Result ρ_A = ½|0⟩⟨0| + ½|1⟩⟨1| = I/2, the maximally mixed one-qubit state.
ρ_A is mixed although ρ is pure, so mixedness is not the same as classical randomness.
Tr(ρ_A²) = ½ < 1 confirms mixedness; no local measurement can recover the correlations.

bank.q: Show that the four Bell states form an orthonormal basis of the two-qubit space, and prove that each is entangled.
outline: Compute inner products to show orthonormality; count four states in a four-dimensional space.
Proof of entanglement: assume (a|0⟩+b|1⟩)⊗(c|0⟩+d|1⟩) and compare coefficients.
For |Φ⁺⟩ the conditions ac ≠ 0, bd ≠ 0 and ad = bc = 0 contradict each other.
Note that Bell states are produced by H on one qubit followed by CNOT.

bank.q: Derive the CHSH inequality |S| ≤ 2 for a local hidden-variable model and show that quantum mechanics gives S = 2√2.
outline: Define E(a,b) = P(same) − P(different) for measurement settings a, a′ on one side and b, b′ on the other.
Local hidden variables: each outcome is a function of the setting and the hidden variable λ, with a shared distribution.
Use the algebraic identity showing S = ±2 at worst for each λ, hence |⟨S⟩| ≤ 2.
Quantum case: choose observables A₀ = Z, A₁ = X, B₀ = (Z+X)/√2, B₁ = (Z−X)/√2 on |Φ⁺⟩.
Each E evaluates to ±1/√2, giving S = 2√2, above the classical bound and at the Tsirelson limit.

bank.q: Explain the CHSH game. Compute the best classical winning probability and the best quantum winning probability, and discuss what the gap proves.
outline: Rules: referee gives bits x, y; players reply a, b; they win when a ⊕ b = x·y.
Classical: a deterministic strategy wins on 3 of 4 input pairs, so p ≤ 0.75.
Quantum: share |Φ⁺⟩, measure at angles depending on the received bit.
The quantum strategy wins with p = cos²(π/8) ≈ 0.854.
Conclusion: no local hidden-variable model reproduces the statistics; the gap is a device-independent test of entanglement.

bank.q: Using the postulates, show step by step that measurement on one half of an entangled pair instantly fixes the state of the other half, and explain why no signal travels.
outline: Start from |Φ⁺⟩ and apply the measurement postulate with projectors P₀ = |0⟩⟨0|⊗I and P₁ = |1⟩⟨1|⊗I.
Outcome probabilities are ½ each; the post-measurement states are |00⟩ and |11⟩.
The remote qubit becomes |0⟩ or |1⟩ correlated with the outcome, so the joint state is a product afterwards.
The reduced state of the remote qubit is I/2 before and after, so its local statistics do not change.
No-signalling: the sender cannot choose the outcome, so no message is transmitted; explaining the correlation needs a classical channel.

bank.q: Compare the state-vector and density-operator descriptions of a qubit. When is a density operator necessary, and how do you test purity?
outline: State vector describes only pure states; density operator describes pure and mixed states.
Properties of ρ: Hermitian, positive semi-definite, Tr ρ = 1; pure iff Tr(ρ²) = 1.
Bloch picture: ρ = (I + r·σ)/2 with |r| ≤ 1; |r| = 1 pure, |r| < 1 mixed, r = 0 maximally mixed.
Mixed states arise from entanglement with an unobserved system, from noise, or from ignorance in an ensemble.
Measurement statistics p(m) = Tr(Pₘρ) reduce to the Born rule for pure states.

bank.q: Discuss the EPR argument and Bell's reply. What assumptions does Bell's theorem rule out, and what loopholes remain in experiments?
outline: EPR: perfect correlations plus locality plus no disturbance seem to force pre-existing values (elements of reality).
Bell: any model with local hidden variables must obey an inequality; quantum mechanics predicts a violation.
Assumptions tested: locality, realism (pre-existing definite values), and freedom of setting choice.
Experiments with entangled photons see the violation, closing the locality loophole with fast switching.
Remaining loopholes and interpretations: detection efficiency, superdeterminism, many-worlds versus collapse readings.

bank.q: Explain the uncertainty principle for two observables, derive ΔA·ΔB ≥ ½|⟨[A,B]⟩|, and connect it to non-commuting Pauli matrices.
outline: Define variance ΔA² = ⟨A²⟩ − ⟨A⟩² for a state |ψ⟩.
Use the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality on the vectors (A − ⟨A⟩)|ψ⟩ and (B − ⟨B⟩)|ψ⟩.
Insert the commutator and anticommutator to obtain ΔA·ΔB ≥ ½|⟨[A,B]⟩|.
For Pauli matrices [σx, σy] = 2iσz, so Δσx·Δσy ≥ |⟨σz⟩|.
Implication: a state with sharp x-spin has completely uncertain z-spin, exactly as sequential Stern–Gerlach shows.

glossary.def: A complete complex vector space with an inner product; quantum state vectors live in it.
The bra-ket notation in which |ψ⟩ is a vector and ⟨ψ| is its conjugate transpose.
A set of linearly independent vectors that spans the space, so every state is a unique combination of them.
A basis whose vectors have unit norm and zero inner product with each other.
A two-level quantum system whose pure states are unit vectors in a two-dimensional complex space.
A complex coefficient in a superposition; its squared modulus gives a measurement probability.
A factor e^{iγ} multiplying the whole state vector; it changes nothing observable.
The phase difference between two amplitudes in a superposition; it is observable through interference.
An operator U with U†U = I; it preserves inner products and describes closed-system evolution.
An operator with A† = A; it has real eigenvalues and represents an observable.
A Hermitian operator whose eigenvalues are the possible measurement outcomes.
An operator P with P² = P and P† = P; it picks out a subspace, and a projective measurement uses orthogonal projectors.
The rule p(m) = ⟨ψ|Pₘ|ψ⟩ giving the probability of each measurement outcome.
The change of the state to Pₘ|ψ⟩/√p(m) immediately after an outcome m is recorded.
The unit sphere whose points label all pure single-qubit states by angles θ and φ.
A positive Hermitian operator with trace one that describes pure and mixed states and yields p(m) = Tr(Pₘρ).
A state that can be written as a single vector, equivalently one with Tr(ρ²) = 1.
A statistical mixture of states, with Tr(ρ²) < 1; it has no single state vector.
The ⊗ construction that combines two state spaces into a joint space of multiplied dimension.
The operation that removes one subsystem from a joint density operator, giving the reduced state of the rest.
A joint state that cannot be factored into a product of states of its parts.
Any of the four maximally entangled two-qubit states built from |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩ with ± signs.
A pre-existing value carried by each particle that fixes its outcome for any setting, shared through a common λ.
The bound |S| ≤ 2 that every local hidden-variable model obeys for the four-setting correlation combination S.
The principle that local measurement statistics on one side of an entangled pair do not depend on what is done on the other side.
